Implement `src/index.js` so it exports `TableError`, `stringWidth`, `wrapCell`, `padCell` and `formatTable`. `TableError` extends `Error`, sets `name` to `'TableError'`, carries a `code` string, and is constructed as `(code, message)`. Everything below measures text in terminal columns, never in code units, so iterate by code point.

`stringWidth(text)` returns the column count of a string, throwing `'BAD_CELL'` with message `cell must be a string` for a non-string. A code point below U+0020, U+007F, any of U+200B, U+200C, U+200D and U+FEFF, or anything in U+0300 to U+036F counts as 0 columns. A code point in any of these inclusive ranges counts as 2 columns: U+1100-U+115F, U+2E80-U+303E, U+3041-U+33FF, U+3400-U+4DBF, U+4E00-U+9FFF, U+A000-U+A4CF, U+AC00-U+D7A3, U+F900-U+FAFF, U+FE10-U+FE19, U+FE30-U+FE6F, U+FF00-U+FF60, U+FFE0-U+FFE6, U+1F300-U+1F64F, U+1F900-U+1F9FF, U+20000-U+2FFFD and U+30000-U+3FFFD. Everything else counts as 1.

`wrapCell(text, width)` returns the lines a cell occupies in a column of `width` columns, always at least one line, and never a line wider than `width`. `width` must be an integer of at least 1 (`'BAD_WIDTH'`, `width must be a positive integer`) and `text` must be a string (`'BAD_CELL'`, `cell must be a string`). The text is first split on newlines and each piece wrapped on its own, so an empty piece contributes one empty line. Within a piece, runs of one or more spaces separate words and collapse to a single space; leading and trailing spaces disappear, and a piece with no words yields one empty line. A word wider than the column is broken greedily into chunks of at most `width` columns, so a 2-column character that would straddle the edge starts the next chunk and leaves the previous one a column short; a single character wider than the whole column throws `'UNWRAPPABLE'` with message `character is wider than the column`. Words and chunks are then packed greedily, one space between neighbours on the same line, starting a new line whenever the next word would push the line past `width`.

`padCell(text, width, align)` pads one already-fitting line to exactly `width` columns, with `align` defaulting to `'left'` and also accepting `'right'` and `'center'`; centring puts the smaller half of the padding on the left. It throws `'BAD_CELL'` for a non-string, `'BAD_WIDTH'` with message `width must be a positive integer` for a bad width, `'BAD_ALIGN'` with message `unknown alignment: <align>` for anything else, and `'CELL_TOO_WIDE'` with message `content is wider than the column` when the text does not fit. `formatTable(rows, options)` renders `rows`, an array of arrays of strings, using `options.widths` (an array of positive integers, one per column), the optional `options.align` (one alignment per column, all `'left'` by default) and the optional boolean `options.header`. Validation runs in this order, each failure throwing immediately: `options` must be a non-null object (`'BAD_OPTIONS'`, `options must be an object`); `widths` must be a non-empty array of positive integers (`'BAD_WIDTH'`, `widths must be a non-empty array of positive integers`); `align`, when given, must be an array of the same length (`'BAD_ALIGN'`, `align must have <n> entries`) holding known alignments (`'BAD_ALIGN'`, `unknown alignment: <value>`); `rows` must be an array (`'BAD_ROWS'`, `rows must be an array`); and each row, in order, must have one cell per column (`'BAD_ROW_LENGTH'`, `row <i> has <n> cells, expected <m>`, counting a non-array row as 0 cells) with every cell a string (`'BAD_CELL'`, `cell at row <i>, column <j> is not a string`). No rows renders the empty string. Otherwise every cell is wrapped to its column, a row occupies as many lines as its tallest cell with the shorter cells padded out with blanks, and the cells of one line are padded and joined with ` | `. When `header` is true a rule of hyphens per column joined with `-+-` follows the first row. Lines are joined with newlines, with no trailing newline, and every line of the result has the same display width. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

Everything below measures text in terminal columns, never in code units, so iterate by code point.

`stringWidth(text)` returns the column count of a string, throwing `'BAD_CELL'` with message `cell must be a string` for a non-string. A code point below U+0020, U+007F, any of U+200B, U+200C, U+200D and U+FEFF, or anything in U+0300 to U+036F counts as 0 columns. A code point in any of these inclusive ranges counts as 2 columns: U+1100-U+115F, U+2E80-U+303E, U+3041-U+33FF, U+3400-U+4DBF, U+4E00-U+9FFF, U+A000-U+A4CF, U+AC00-U+D7A3, U+F900-U+FAFF, U+FE10-U+FE19, U+FE30-U+FE6F, U+FF00-U+FF60, U+FFE0-U+FFE6, U+1F300-U+1F64F, U+1F900-U+1F9FF, U+20000-U+2FFFD and U+30000-U+3FFFD. Everything else counts as 1.

`wrapCell(text, width)` returns the lines a cell occupies in a column of `width` columns, always at least one line, and never a line wider than `width`. `width` must be an integer of at least 1 (`'BAD_WIDTH'`, `width must be a positive integer`) and `text` must be a string (`'BAD_CELL'`, `cell must be a string`). The text is first split on newlines and each piece wrapped on its own, so an empty piece contributes one empty line. Within a piece, runs of one or more spaces separate words and collapse to a single space; leading and trailing spaces disappear, and a piece with no words yields one empty line. A word wider than the column is broken greedily into chunks of at most `width` columns, so a 2-column character that would straddle the edge starts the next chunk and leaves the previous one a column short; a single character wider than the whole column throws `'UNWRAPPABLE'` with message `character is wider than the column`. Words and chunks are then packed greedily, one space between neighbours on the same line, starting a new line whenever the next word would push the line past `width`.

`padCell(text, width, align)` pads one already-fitting line to exactly `width` columns, with `align` defaulting to `'left'` and also accepting `'right'` and `'center'`; centring puts the smaller half of the padding on the left. It throws `'BAD_CELL'` for a non-string, `'BAD_WIDTH'` with message `width must be a positive integer` for a bad width, `'BAD_ALIGN'` with message `unknown alignment: <align>` for anything else, and `'CELL_TOO_WIDE'` with message `content is wider than the column` when the text does not fit. `formatTable(rows, options)` renders `rows`, an array of arrays of strings, using `options.widths` (an array of positive integers, one per column), the optional `options.align` (one alignment per column, all `'left'` by default) and the optional boolean `options.header`. Validation runs in this order, each failure throwing immediately: `options` must be a non-null object (`'BAD_OPTIONS'`, `options must be an object`); `widths` must be a non-empty array of positive integers (`'BAD_WIDTH'`, `widths must be a non-empty array of positive integers`); `align`, when given, must be an array of the same length (`'BAD_ALIGN'`, `align must have <n> entries`) holding known alignments (`'BAD_ALIGN'`, `unknown alignment: <value>`); `rows` must be an array (`'BAD_ROWS'`, `rows must be an array`); and each row, in order, must have one cell per column (`'BAD_ROW_LENGTH'`, `row <i> has <n> cells, expected <m>`, counting a non-array row as 0 cells) with every cell a string (`'BAD_CELL'`, `cell at row <i>, column <j> is not a string`). No rows renders the empty string. Otherwise every cell is wrapped to its column, a row occupies as many lines as its tallest cell with the shorter cells padded out with blanks, and the cells of one line are padded and joined with ` | `. When `header` is true a rule of hyphens per column joined with `-+-` follows the first row. Lines are joined with newlines, with no trailing newline, and every line of the result has the same display width. Change only files under src/. Implement `src/index.js` so it exports `PathError`, `isAbsolute`, `normalize`, `join` and `relative`. This module does pure string arithmetic over POSIX-style paths: it never touches the filesystem, never consults the working directory, and never imports another path library. `PathError` extends `Error`, sets `name` to `'PathError'`, carries a `code` string and is constructed as `(code, message)`. Every argument of every function must be a string, otherwise the call throws `'NOT_A_STRING'` with message `path must be a string`, and no argument may contain a NUL character (U+0000), otherwise the call throws `'NUL_BYTE'` with message `path contains a NUL byte`. These two checks run before anything else, left to right over the arguments.

`isAbsolute(path)` reports whether the path begins with a slash; the empty string is not absolute. `normalize(path)` rejects the empty string with `'EMPTY_PATH'` and message `path must not be empty`, then splits the path on slashes and walks the segments left to right, dropping empty segments (so repeated and trailing slashes disappear) and `.` segments. A `..` segment pops the previous segment when there is one to pop. On a rooted path a `..` that would climb above the root throws `'ESCAPE'` with message `path escapes root: <the original argument>`; on a relative path such a `..` is kept, so leading parent segments survive. The result of a rooted path is a slash followed by the remaining segments, so the root itself normalizes to `/`; the result of a relative path is the remaining segments joined by slashes, or `.` when none are left. A normalized path never contains two consecutive slashes and never ends in a slash unless it is exactly `/`. Names beginning with a dot, such as `.hidden`, `..a` and `...`, are ordinary segments.

`join(...segments)` requires at least one segment (`'NO_SEGMENTS'`, `join requires at least one segment`). Each segment is checked in order: it must not be the empty string (`'EMPTY_SEGMENT'`, `segment <index> must not be empty`, index counted from 0), and no segment after the first may begin with a slash (`'ABSOLUTE_SEGMENT'`, `segment <index> must be relative`). The segments are then joined with single slashes and the result normalized, so joining can itself raise `'ESCAPE'`.

`relative(from, to)` returns the relative path that leads from the first location to the second. Both arguments must be absolute, otherwise it throws `'NOT_ABSOLUTE'` with message `both paths must be absolute`. Both are normalized first, so an escaping argument raises `'ESCAPE'`. The longest common run of leading segments is dropped, and the answer is one `..` per remaining segment of `from` followed by the remaining segments of `to`, joined by slashes. Two equal paths give the empty string. The result is always relative, always already normalized, and joining it back onto `from` (using `.` in place of the empty string) reproduces `to`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

Implement `src/index.js` so it exports `PathError`, `isAbsolute`, `normalize`, `join` and `relative`. This module does pure string arithmetic over POSIX-style paths: it never touches the filesystem, never consults the working directory, and never imports another path library. `PathError` extends `Error`, sets `name` to `'PathError'`, carries a `code` string and is constructed as `(code, message)`. These two checks run before anything else, left to right over the arguments.

`isAbsolute(path)` reports whether the path begins with a slash; the empty string is not absolute. `normalize(path)` rejects the empty string with `'EMPTY_PATH'` and message `path must not be empty`, then splits the path on slashes and walks the segments left to right, dropping empty segments (so repeated and trailing slashes disappear) and `.` segments. A `..` segment pops the previous segment when there is one to pop. On a rooted path a `..` that would climb above the root throws `'ESCAPE'` with message `path escapes root: <the original argument>`; on a relative path such a `..` is kept, so leading parent segments survive. The result of a rooted path is a slash followed by the remaining segments, so the root itself normalizes to `/`; the result of a relative path is the remaining segments joined by slashes, or `.` when none are left. A normalized path never contains two consecutive slashes and never ends in a slash unless it is exactly `/`. Names beginning with a dot, such as `.hidden`, `..a` and `...`, are ordinary segments.

`join(...segments)` requires at least one segment (`'NO_SEGMENTS'`, `join requires at least one segment`). Each segment is checked in order: it must not be the empty string (`'EMPTY_SEGMENT'`, `segment <index> must not be empty`, index counted from 0), and no segment after the first may begin with a slash (`'ABSOLUTE_SEGMENT'`, `segment <index> must be relative`). The segments are then joined with single slashes and the result normalized, so joining can itself raise `'ESCAPE'`.

`relative(from, to)` returns the relative path that leads from the first location to the second. Both arguments must be absolute, otherwise it throws `'NOT_ABSOLUTE'` with message `both paths must be absolute`. Both are normalized first, so an escaping argument raises `'ESCAPE'`. The longest common run of leading segments is dropped, and the answer is one `..` per remaining segment of `from` followed by the remaining segments of `to`, joined by slashes. Two equal paths give the empty string. The result is always relative, always already normalized, and joining it back onto `from` (using `.` in place of the empty string) reproduces `to`. Implement `src/intervals.js`, a set algebra over half-open integer intervals. An interval is a two-element array `[start, end)` of safe integers that covers every integer x with `start <= x < end`. An interval list is normalised when it is sorted by start, contains no empty interval, and no two of its members overlap or touch: `[1, 3)` and `[3, 5)` touch and must coalesce into `[1, 5)`, while `[1, 3)` and `[4, 5)` must stay apart.

Export five functions. `normalize(intervals)` returns the normalised form of one list. `merge(a, b)` returns the normalised union of two lists. `intersect(a, b)` returns the normalised intersection; touching intervals share no integer, so `[1, 3)` against `[3, 5)` yields an empty list. `subtract(a, b)` returns the normalised relative complement `a \ b`. `coverage(intervals)` returns how many integers the list covers, counting an integer covered by several intervals once.

Every function validates both of its interval-list arguments before doing any work, and inputs may be adversarial: unsorted, duplicated, nested, negative, empty (`start === end`, which normalisation drops), or spanning a large range. A value that is not an array raises `TypeError` with message `interval list must be an array`. A member that is not a two-element array raises `TypeError` with message `interval must be a two-element array`. A bound that is not a safe integer — a float, a numeric string, `NaN`, `Infinity`, or a value beyond `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` — raises `TypeError` with message `interval bounds must be safe integers`. An interval whose start exceeds its end raises `RangeError` with message `interval start must not exceed end`.

No function may mutate its arguments or return arrays that alias them; every returned interval is freshly allocated. 11: /**
12:  * Deterministic 32-bit PRNG.
13:  * @param {number} seed Initial state.
14:  * @returns {() => number} Generator returning floats in [0, 1).
15:  */
16: function mulberry32(seed) {
17:   let a = seed >>> 0;
18:   return () => {
19:     a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) >>> 0;
20:     let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
21:     t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
22:     return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
23:   };
24: }

26: /**
27:  * Rasterises an interval list over the model universe.
28:  * @param {Array<[number, number]>} list Interval list.
29:  * @returns {Uint8Array} One byte per integer in [LO, HI).
30:  */
31: function raster(list) {
32:   const bits = new Uint8Array(HI - LO);
33:   for (const [start, end] of list) {
34:     for (let x = Math.max(start, LO); x < Math.min(end, HI); x += 1) bits[x - LO] = 1;
35:   }
36:   return bits;

goal.objective:
Implement `src/intervals.js`, a set algebra over half-open integer intervals. An interval is a two-element array `[start, end)` of safe integers that covers every integer x with `start <= x < end`. An interval list is normalised when it is sorted by start, contains no empty interval, and no two of its members overlap or touch: `[1, 3)` and `[3, 5)` touch and must coalesce into `[1, 5)`, while `[1, 3)` and `[4, 5)` must stay apart.

Export five functions. `normalize(intervals)` returns the normalised form of one list. `merge(a, b)` returns the normalised union of two lists. `intersect(a, b)` returns the normalised intersection; touching intervals share no integer, so `[1, 3)` against `[3, 5)` yields an empty list. `subtract(a, b)` returns the normalised relative complement `a \ b`. `coverage(intervals)` returns how many integers the list covers, counting an integer covered by several intervals once.

Every function validates both of its interval-list arguments before doing any work, and inputs may be adversarial: unsorted, duplicated, nested, negative, empty (`start === end`, which normalisation drops), or spanning a large range. A value that is not an array raises `TypeError` with message `interval list must be an array`. A member that is not a two-element array raises `TypeError` with message `interval must be a two-element array`. A bound that is not a safe integer — a float, a numeric string, `NaN`, `Infinity`, or a value beyond `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` — raises `TypeError` with message `interval bounds must be safe integers`. An interval whose start exceeds its end raises `RangeError` with message `interval start must not exceed end`.

No function may mutate its arguments or return arrays that alias them; every returned interval is freshly allocated. Do not add dependencies; `test/` and `package.json` are fixed and the suite must pass with `node --test test/*.test.js`. Change only files under src/. Implement `src/index.js` so it exports `PathError`, `isAbsolute`, `normalize`, `join` and `relative`. This module does pure string arithmetic over POSIX-style paths: it never touches the filesystem, never consults the working directory, and never imports another path library. `PathError` extends `Error`, sets `name` to `'PathError'`, carries a `code` string and is constructed as `(code, message)`. Every argument of every function must be a string, otherwise the call throws `'NOT_A_STRING'` with message `path must be a string`, and no argument may contain a NUL character (U+0000), otherwise the call throws `'NUL_BYTE'` with message `path contains a NUL byte`. These two checks run before anything else, left to right over the arguments.

`isAbsolute(path)` reports whether the path begins with a slash; the empty string is not absolute. `normalize(path)` rejects the empty string with `'EMPTY_PATH'` and message `path must not be empty`, then splits the path on slashes and walks the segments left to right, dropping empty segments (so repeated and trailing slashes disappear) and `.` segments. A `..` segment pops the previous segment when there is one to pop. On a rooted path a `..` that would climb above the root throws `'ESCAPE'` with message `path escapes root: <the original argument>`; on a relative path such a `..` is kept, so leading parent segments survive. The result of a rooted path is a slash followed by the remaining segments, so the root itself normalizes to `/`; the result of a relative path is the remaining segments joined by slashes, or `.` when none are left. A normalized path never contains two consecutive slashes and never ends in a slash unless it is exactly `/`. Names beginning with a dot, such as `.hidden`, `..a` and `...`, are ordinary segments.

`join(...segments)` requires at least one segment (`'NO_SEGMENTS'`, `join requires at least one segment`). Each segment is checked in order: it must not be the empty string (`'EMPTY_SEGMENT'`, `segment <index> must not be empty`, index counted from 0), and no segment after the first may begin with a slash (`'ABSOLUTE_SEGMENT'`, `segment <index> must be relative`). The segments are then joined with single slashes and the result normalized, so joining can itself raise `'ESCAPE'`.

`relative(from, to)` returns the relative path that leads from the first location to the second. Both arguments must be absolute, otherwise it throws `'NOT_ABSOLUTE'` with message `both paths must be absolute`. Both are normalized first, so an escaping argument raises `'ESCAPE'`. The longest common run of leading segments is dropped, and the answer is one `..` per remaining segment of `from` followed by the remaining segments of `to`, joined by slashes. Two equal paths give the empty string. The result is always relative, always already normalized, and joining it back onto `from` (using `.` in place of the empty string) reproduces `to`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

These two checks run before anything else, left to right over the arguments.

`isAbsolute(path)` reports whether the path begins with a slash; the empty string is not absolute. `normalize(path)` rejects the empty string with `'EMPTY_PATH'` and message `path must not be empty`, then splits the path on slashes and walks the segments left to right, dropping empty segments (so repeated and trailing slashes disappear) and `.` segments. A `..` segment pops the previous segment when there is one to pop. On a rooted path a `..` that would climb above the root throws `'ESCAPE'` with message `path escapes root: <the original argument>`; on a relative path such a `..` is kept, so leading parent segments survive. The result of a rooted path is a slash followed by the remaining segments, so the root itself normalizes to `/`; the result of a relative path is the remaining segments joined by slashes, or `.` when none are left. A normalized path never contains two consecutive slashes and never ends in a slash unless it is exactly `/`. Names beginning with a dot, such as `.hidden`, `..a` and `...`, are ordinary segments.

`join(...segments)` requires at least one segment (`'NO_SEGMENTS'`, `join requires at least one segment`). `src/csv.js` must export `parse`, `stringify`, `escapeField` and the error class `CsvError`. `parse(text, options)` returns an array of records, each an array of field strings. A leading U+FEFF byte-order mark is dropped; anywhere else U+FEFF is ordinary data. Records are terminated by CRLF, LF or a lone CR, and a single terminator at the very end of the document closes the last record without starting an empty one, so `"a\n"` and `"a"` both read as one record while `"a\n\n"` reads as two and `"\n"` reads as one record holding one empty field. An empty document has no records at all. Fields are never trimmed, and an empty field is preserved wherever it appears, including at the start or end of a record.

A field is quoted only when the quote character is its very first character: there, the field runs to the matching closing quote, a doubled quote character stands for one literal quote, and delimiters and line terminators inside the quotes are data rather than separators. A quote character anywhere else in a field is ordinary text. After a closing quote only a delimiter, a line terminator or the end of the document may follow. `options.delimiter` (default `,`) and `options.quote` (default `"`) each take one UTF-16 code unit; they must differ from each other and neither may be a line terminator. `options.strictWidth` makes every record after the first have to match the first record's field count; without it ragged records are returned as they are.

content.text:
Implement `src/sortBy.js`, a stable multi-key sort for arrays of records. A key spec is an object `{ key, direction, nulls }`. `key` is either a function that reads the value out of a row, or a dot-separated property path such as `'user.last'` where a missing or nullish step yields `undefined`. `direction` is `'asc'` (the default) or `'desc'`. `nulls` is `'last'` (the default) or `'first'`.

Export four functions. `compareValues(a, b)` is the underlying total order over single values. `comparator(specs)` returns a comparator over rows that applies the specs in order. `sortIndices(rows, specs)` returns the permutation of indices that sorts the rows. `sortBy(rows, specs)` returns a new array of the rows in sorted order; it must not mutate its argument, and it must be stable, so rows that compare equal on every key keep their input order — in both directions, since a descending sort is not a reversed ascending sort.

Ordering is locale-free. `null`, `undefined`, and `NaN` all count as absent; absent values are equal to each other, and where they land is decided by `nulls` alone, never by `direction`, so `{ direction: 'desc', nulls: 'last' }` still puts them at the end. `compareValues` itself places absent values before every present value. Present values of the same type compare as follows: numbers numerically, with `-0` equal to `0`; strings by Unicode code point, so a code point above the basic plane sorts after `U+FFFD` and never by UTF-16 code unit, and never with `localeCompare`; booleans with `false` before `true`. When one key holds several types, order by type: numbers, then strings, then booleans. Any other type of value — an object, an array, a function, a bigint, a symbol — raises `TypeError` with message `unsupported value type: object`, naming the offending `typeof`.

Validation happens before any comparison. Rows that are not an array raise `TypeError` with message `rows must be an array`. A spec list that is not a non-empty array raises `TypeError` with message `at least one key spec is required`. A spec that is not an object raises `TypeError` with message `key spec must be an object`, and one whose key is neither a string nor a function raises `TypeError` with message `key must be a string path or a function`. An unknown direction raises `RangeError` with message `unknown direction: "up"` and an unknown null placement raises `RangeError` with message `unknown null placement: "middle"`, each quoting the offending value as JSON. Do not add dependencies; `test/` and `package.json` are fixed and the suite must pass with `node --test test/*.test.js`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

A key spec is an object `{ key, direction, nulls }`. `key` is either a function that reads the value out of a row, or a dot-separated property path such as `'user.last'` where a missing or nullish step yields `undefined`. `direction` is `'asc'` (the default) or `'desc'`. `nulls` is `'last'` (the default) or `'first'`.

Export four functions. `compareValues(a, b)` is the underlying total order over single values. `comparator(specs)` returns a comparator over rows that applies the specs in order. `sortIndices(rows, specs)` returns the permutation of indices that sorts the rows. `sortBy(rows, specs)` returns a new array of the rows in sorted order; it must not mutate its argument, and it must be stable, so rows that compare equal on every key keep their input order — in both directions, since a descending sort is not a reversed ascending sort.

`src/glob.js` must export `compile`, `isMatch`, `filter` and the error class `GlobError`. `compile(pattern, options)` returns a function that reports whether a whole path matches; `isMatch(path, pattern, options)` is the one-shot form, and `filter(paths, pattern, options)` keeps the matching paths in their original order without removing duplicates. Paths are separated by `/` and a pattern is anchored at both ends. Within one segment, `*` matches any run of characters other than `/`, including none, and `?` matches exactly one character other than `/`; a run of several `*` in a segment behaves as one.

A segment that is exactly `**` matches zero or more whole segments, so `a/**/b` matches `a/b`, `a/x/b` and `a/x/y/b` but not `a/b/c`, `**/a` matches `a` and `x/y/a`, `a/**` matches `a` as well as `a/b/c`, and adjacent `**` segments collapse into one. A bracket expression matches one character: `[abc]` and ranges such as `[a-c]` match a listed character, while `[!...]` and `[^...]` match one character that is neither `/` nor listed. A `]` written immediately after the opening bracket, or after the negation mark, is a literal `]`, a `-` at either end of the list is a literal `-`, and a backslash inside the brackets escapes the next character. Outside brackets a backslash also removes the special meaning of the next character, so `\*` matches a literal asterisk. Characters that are special to regular expressions but not to globs, such as `.`, `+`, `(` and `$`, always stand for themselves.

A path segment that begins with `.` is matched only by a pattern segment that itself begins with a literal `.` (optionally written as `\.`): `*`, `?`, `**` and a bracket expression all refuse a leading dot, so `*` does not match `.x`, `**/y` does not match `.x/y`, and `[.]x` does not match `.x`, while `.*` does. `options.dot` set to true removes that restriction everywhere. `options.nocase` set to true makes matching case-insensitive. `src/csv.js` must export `parse`, `stringify`, `escapeField` and the error class `CsvError`. `parse(text, options)` returns an array of records, each an array of field strings. A leading U+FEFF byte-order mark is dropped; anywhere else U+FEFF is ordinary data. Records are terminated by CRLF, LF or a lone CR, and a single terminator at the very end of the document closes the last record without starting an empty one, so `"a\n"` and `"a"` both read as one record while `"a\n\n"` reads as two and `"\n"` reads as one record holding one empty field. An empty document has no records at all. Fields are never trimmed, and an empty field is preserved wherever it appears, including at the start or end of a record.

A field is quoted only when the quote character is its very first character: there, the field runs to the matching closing quote, a doubled quote character stands for one literal quote, and delimiters and line terminators inside the quotes are data rather than separators. A quote character anywhere else in a field is ordinary text. After a closing quote only a delimiter, a line terminator or the end of the document may follow. `options.delimiter` (default `,`) and `options.quote` (default `"`) each take one UTF-16 code unit; they must differ from each other and neither may be a line terminator. `options.strictWidth` makes every record after the first have to match the first record's field count; without it ragged records are returned as they are.

Every failure throws `CsvError`. Positional failures carry a 1-based `line` and, where a single character is at fault, a 1-based `column` counted in UTF-16 code units from the start of that line: `unterminated quoted field` points at the opening quote, and `unexpected character after closing quote: b` points at the offending character, both accounting for line breaks that occurred inside a quoted field. `expected 2 fields, got 1` carries the line the offending record starts on. Bad arguments throw without a position: `input must be a string`, `delimiter must be a single character`, `quote must be a single character`, `delimiter and quote must differ`, `delimiter and quote must not be line terminators`.

`escapeField(value, options)` returns the text for one field. A string is used as it is; `null` and `undefined` become the empty field; booleans and finite numbers are converted with `String`; anything else throws (`unsupported field value: NaN` for non-finite numbers, `unsupported field type: object` otherwise). The field is quoted, doubling every embedded quote character, when it contains the delimiter, the quote character, CR, LF or U+FEFF, or when `options.alwaysQuote` is set. `stringify(rows, options)` writes each record's escaped fields joined by the delimiter and followed by `options.newline` (default CRLF, and it must be CRLF, LF or CR), including after the last record, and prepends the byte-order mark when `options.bom` is set. `stringify` throws `CsvError` for input that is not an array (`rows must be an array`), a record that is not an array (`record 1 is not an array`) and a record with no fields (`record 0 has no fields`). goal.objective:
`src/csv.js` must export `parse`, `stringify`, `escapeField` and the error class `CsvError`. `parse(text, options)` returns an array of records, each an array of field strings. A leading U+FEFF byte-order mark is dropped; anywhere else U+FEFF is ordinary data. Records are terminated by CRLF, LF or a lone CR, and a single terminator at the very end of the document closes the last record without starting an empty one, so `"a\n"` and `"a"` both read as one record while `"a\n\n"` reads as two and `"\n"` reads as one record holding one empty field. An empty document has no records at all. Fields are never trimmed, and an empty field is preserved wherever it appears, including at the start or end of a record.

A field is quoted only when the quote character is its very first character: there, the field runs to the matching closing quote, a doubled quote character stands for one literal quote, and delimiters and line terminators inside the quotes are data rather than separators. A quote character anywhere else in a field is ordinary text. After a closing quote only a delimiter, a line terminator or the end of the document may follow. `options.delimiter` (default `,`) and `options.quote` (default `"`) each take one UTF-16 code unit; they must differ from each other and neither may be a line terminator. `options.strictWidth` makes every record after the first have to match the first record's field count; without it ragged records are returned as they are.

Every failure throws `CsvError`. Positional failures carry a 1-based `line` and, where a single character is at fault, a 1-based `column` counted in UTF-16 code units from the start of that line: `unterminated quoted field` points at the opening quote, and `unexpected character after closing quote: b` points at the offending character, both accounting for line breaks that occurred inside a quoted field. `expected 2 fields, got 1` carries the line the offending record starts on. Bad arguments throw without a position: `input must be a string`, `delimiter must be a single character`, `quote must be a single character`, `delimiter and quote must differ`, `delimiter and quote must not be line terminators`.

`escapeField(value, options)` returns the text for one field. A string is used as it is; `null` and `undefined` become the empty field; booleans and finite numbers are converted with `String`; anything else throws (`unsupported field value: NaN` for non-finite numbers, `unsupported field type: object` otherwise). The field is quoted, doubling every embedded quote character, when it contains the delimiter, the quote character, CR, LF or U+FEFF, or when `options.alwaysQuote` is set. `stringify(rows, options)` writes each record's escaped fields joined by the delimiter and followed by `options.newline` (default CRLF, and it must be CRLF, LF or CR), including after the last record, and prepends the byte-order mark when `options.bom` is set. `stringify` throws `CsvError` for input that is not an array (`rows must be an array`), a record that is not an array (`record 1 is not an array`) and a record with no fields (`record 0 has no fields`). Reading a document this module wrote, with the same options, must return exactly the records it was given. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

Implement `src/intervals.js`, a set algebra over half-open integer intervals. An interval is a two-element array `[start, end)` of safe integers that covers every integer x with `start <= x < end`. An interval list is normalised when it is sorted by start, contains no empty interval, and no two of its members overlap or touch: `[1, 3)` and `[3, 5)` touch and must coalesce into `[1, 5)`, while `[1, 3)` and `[4, 5)` must stay apart.

Export five functions. `normalize(intervals)` returns the normalised form of one list. `merge(a, b)` returns the normalised union of two lists. `intersect(a, b)` returns the normalised intersection; touching intervals share no integer, so `[1, 3)` against `[3, 5)` yields an empty list. `subtract(a, b)` returns the normalised relative complement `a \ b`. `coverage(intervals)` returns how many integers the list covers, counting an integer covered by several intervals once.

Every function validates both of its interval-list arguments before doing any work, and inputs may be adversarial: unsorted, duplicated, nested, negative, empty (`start === end`, which normalisation drops), or spanning a large range. A value that is not an array raises `TypeError` with message `interval list must be an array`. A member that is not a two-element array raises `TypeError` with message `interval must be a two-element array`. A bound that is not a safe integer — a float, a numeric string, `NaN`, `Infinity`, or a value beyond `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` — raises `TypeError` with message `interval bounds must be safe integers`. An interval whose start exceeds its end raises `RangeError` with message `interval start must not exceed end`.

No function may mutate its arguments or return arrays that alias them; every returned interval is freshly allocated. Do not add dependencies; `test/` and `package.json` are fixed and the suite must pass with `node --test test/*.test.js`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

6: /** Lower bound of the universe used by the model-based checks. */
7: const LO = -40;
8: /** Upper bound (exclusive) of the universe used by the model-based checks. */
9: const HI = 40;
10: 
11: /**
12:  * Deterministic 32-bit PRNG.
13:  * @param {number} seed Initial state.
14:  * @returns {() => number} Generator returning floats in [0, 1).
15:  */
16: function mulberry32(seed) {
17:   let a = seed >>> 0;
18:   return () => {
19:     a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) >>> 0;
20:     let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
21:     t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
22:     return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
23:   };
24: }
25: 
26: /**
27:  * Rasterises an interval list over the model universe.
28:  * @param {Array<[number, number]>} list Interval list.
29:  * @returns {Uint8Array} One byte per integer in [LO, HI).
30:  */
31: function raster(list) {
32:   const bits = new Uint8Array(HI - LO);
33:   for (const [start, end] of list) {
34:     for (let x = Math.max(start, LO); x < Math.min(end, HI); x += 1) bits[x - LO] = 1;
35:   }
36:   return bits;
37: }
38: 
39: /**
40:  * Converts a raster back into a normalised interval list.
41:  * @param {Uint8Array} bits Raster.
42:  * @returns {Array<[number, number]>} Normalised list.
43:  */
44: function unraster(bits) {
45:   const out = [];
46:   let run = -1;
47:   for (let i = 0; i <= bits.length; i += 1) {
48:     const on = i < bits.length && bits[i] === 1;
49:     if (on && run < 0) run = i;
50:     if (!on && run >= 0) {
51:       out.push([run + LO, i + LO]);
52:       run = -1;
53:     }
54:   }
55:   return out;
56: }

66:     assert.ok(list[i][0] < list[i][1], `${label}: empty interval at ${i}`);
67:     if (i > 0) assert.ok(list[i - 1][1] < list[i][0], `${label}: not disjoint at ${i}`);

`src/glob.js` must export `compile`, `isMatch`, `filter` and the error class `GlobError`. `compile(pattern, options)` returns a function that reports whether a whole path matches; `isMatch(path, pattern, options)` is the one-shot form, and `filter(paths, pattern, options)` keeps the matching paths in their original order without removing duplicates. Paths are separated by `/` and a pattern is anchored at both ends. Within one segment, `*` matches any run of characters other than `/`, including none, and `?` matches exactly one character other than `/`; a run of several `*` in a segment behaves as one.

A segment that is exactly `**` matches zero or more whole segments, so `a/**/b` matches `a/b`, `a/x/b` and `a/x/y/b` but not `a/b/c`, `**/a` matches `a` and `x/y/a`, `a/**` matches `a` as well as `a/b/c`, and adjacent `**` segments collapse into one. A bracket expression matches one character: `[abc]` and ranges such as `[a-c]` match a listed character, while `[!...]` and `[^...]` match one character that is neither `/` nor listed. A `]` written immediately after the opening bracket, or after the negation mark, is a literal `]`, a `-` at either end of the list is a literal `-`, and a backslash inside the brackets escapes the next character. Outside brackets a backslash also removes the special meaning of the next character, so `\*` matches a literal asterisk. Characters that are special to regular expressions but not to globs, such as `.`, `+`, `(` and `$`, always stand for themselves.

A path segment that begins with `.` is matched only by a pattern segment that itself begins with a literal `.` (optionally written as `\.`): `*`, `?`, `**` and a bracket expression all refuse a leading dot, so `*` does not match `.x`, `**/y` does not match `.x/y`, and `[.]x` does not match `.x`, while `.*` does. `options.dot` set to true removes that restriction everywhere. `options.nocase` set to true makes matching case-insensitive. Neither option changes anything else.

Every failure throws `GlobError`, and a positional one carries the 0-based `index` into the pattern where the fault starts: `unterminated character class` (index of the opening bracket), `trailing backslash` (index of the backslash), and `path separator in character class` (index of the `/`). An empty pattern (`pattern must not be empty`) and a non-string pattern (`pattern must be a string`) are rejected without an index, as are a non-string path (`path must be a string`) and a non-array first argument to `filter` (`paths must be an array`). Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. Summary of the implementation in `src/glob.js`:

- **`GlobError`**: extends `Error`, carries an optional `index` for positional failures.
- **`parsePattern`**: walks the pattern character by character, building per-segment regex fragments:
  - `\` escapes the next character (throws `trailing backslash` if at end of pattern).
  - `/` ends a segment.
  - Runs of `*` collapse into a single `[^/]*`.
  - `?` becomes `[^/]`.
  - `[...]` bracket expressions are parsed with POSIX rules (leading `]` literal, `!`/`^` negation, `-` handling, backslash escapes inside), throwing `unterminated character class` or `path separator in character class` with the right index.
  - Every other character is regex-escaped as a literal.
  - The leading-dot rule is applied per segment via a `(?!\.)` lookahead prefixed to the first token of a segment, unless that token is itself a literal dot or `options.dot` is set.
- **`collapseGlobstars`**: merges adjacent `**` segments into one.
- **`buildFullSource`**: turns the segment list into a full anchored regex source, handling `**` as zero-or-more whole segments (leading, trailing, middle, and whole-pattern cases), respecting the dot rule for the segments a globstar can expand into.
- **`compile`**: validates pattern type/emptiness, builds the regex (case-insensitive with `i` flag when `nocase` is set), and returns a matcher function that validates the path argument is a string.
- **`isMatch`** and **`filter`**: thin wrappers around `compile`, with `filter` validating `paths` is an array and preserving order/duplicates via `Array.prototype.filter`.

goal.objective:
`src/glob.js` must export `compile`, `isMatch`, `filter` and the error class `GlobError`. `compile(pattern, options)` returns a function that reports whether a whole path matches; `isMatch(path, pattern, options)` is the one-shot form, and `filter(paths, pattern, options)` keeps the matching paths in their original order without removing duplicates. Paths are separated by `/` and a pattern is anchored at both ends. Within one segment, `*` matches any run of characters other than `/`, including none, and `?` matches exactly one character other than `/`; a run of several `*` in a segment behaves as one.

A segment that is exactly `**` matches zero or more whole segments, so `a/**/b` matches `a/b`, `a/x/b` and `a/x/y/b` but not `a/b/c`, `**/a` matches `a` and `x/y/a`, `a/**` matches `a` as well as `a/b/c`, and adjacent `**` segments collapse into one. A bracket expression matches one character: `[abc]` and ranges such as `[a-c]` match a listed character, while `[!...]` and `[^...]` match one character that is neither `/` nor listed. A `]` written immediately after the opening bracket, or after the negation mark, is a literal `]`, a `-` at either end of the list is a literal `-`, and a backslash inside the brackets escapes the next character. Outside brackets a backslash also removes the special meaning of the next character, so `\*` matches a literal asterisk. Characters that are special to regular expressions but not to globs, such as `.`, `+`, `(` and `$`, always stand for themselves.

A path segment that begins with `.` is matched only by a pattern segment that itself begins with a literal `.` (optionally written as `\.`): `*`, `?`, `**` and a bracket expression all refuse a leading dot, so `*` does not match `.x`, `**/y` does not match `.x/y`, and `[.]x` does not match `.x`, while `.*` does. `options.dot` set to true removes that restriction everywhere. `options.nocase` set to true makes matching case-insensitive. Neither option changes anything else.

Every failure throws `GlobError`, and a positional one carries the 0-based `index` into the pattern where the fault starts: `unterminated character class` (index of the opening bracket), `trailing backslash` (index of the backslash), and `path separator in character class` (index of the `/`). An empty pattern (`pattern must not be empty`) and a non-string pattern (`pattern must be a string`) are rejected without an index, as are a non-string path (`path must be a string`) and a non-array first argument to `filter` (`paths must be an array`). Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

Implement `src/sortBy.js`, a stable multi-key sort for arrays of records. A key spec is an object `{ key, direction, nulls }`. `key` is either a function that reads the value out of a row, or a dot-separated property path such as `'user.last'` where a missing or nullish step yields `undefined`. `direction` is `'asc'` (the default) or `'desc'`. `nulls` is `'last'` (the default) or `'first'`.

Export four functions. `compareValues(a, b)` is the underlying total order over single values. `comparator(specs)` returns a comparator over rows that applies the specs in order. `sortIndices(rows, specs)` returns the permutation of indices that sorts the rows. `sortBy(rows, specs)` returns a new array of the rows in sorted order; it must not mutate its argument, and it must be stable, so rows that compare equal on every key keep their input order — in both directions, since a descending sort is not a reversed ascending sort.

Ordering is locale-free. `null`, `undefined`, and `NaN` all count as absent; absent values are equal to each other, and where they land is decided by `nulls` alone, never by `direction`, so `{ direction: 'desc', nulls: 'last' }` still puts them at the end. `compareValues` itself places absent values before every present value. Present values of the same type compare as follows: numbers numerically, with `-0` equal to `0`; strings by Unicode code point, so a code point above the basic plane sorts after `U+FFFD` and never by UTF-16 code unit, and never with `localeCompare`; booleans with `false` before `true`. When one key holds several types, order by type: numbers, then strings, then booleans. Any other type of value — an object, an array, a function, a bigint, a symbol — raises `TypeError` with message `unsupported value type: object`, naming the offending `typeof`.

Validation happens before any comparison. Rows that are not an array raise `TypeError` with message `rows must be an array`. A spec list that is not a non-empty array raises `TypeError` with message `at least one key spec is required`. A spec that is not an object raises `TypeError` with message `key spec must be an object`, and one whose key is neither a string nor a function raises `TypeError` with message `key must be a string path or a function`. An unknown direction raises `RangeError` with message `unknown direction: "up"` and an unknown null placement raises `RangeError` with message `unknown null placement: "middle"`, each quoting the offending value as JSON. Do not add dependencies; `test/` and `package.json` are fixed and the suite must pass with `node --test test/*.test.js`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

goal.objective:
Implement `src/sortBy.js`, a stable multi-key sort for arrays of records. A key spec is an object `{ key, direction, nulls }`. `key` is either a function that reads the value out of a row, or a dot-separated property path such as `'user.last'` where a missing or nullish step yields `undefined`. `direction` is `'asc'` (the default) or `'desc'`. `nulls` is `'last'` (the default) or `'first'`.

Export four functions. `compareValues(a, b)` is the underlying total order over single values. `comparator(specs)` returns a comparator over rows that applies the specs in order. `sortIndices(rows, specs)` returns the permutation of indices that sorts the rows. `sortBy(rows, specs)` returns a new array of the rows in sorted order; it must not mutate its argument, and it must be stable, so rows that compare equal on every key keep their input order — in both directions, since a descending sort is not a reversed ascending sort.

Ordering is locale-free. `null`, `undefined`, and `NaN` all count as absent; absent values are equal to each other, and where they land is decided by `nulls` alone, never by `direction`, so `{ direction: 'desc', nulls: 'last' }` still puts them at the end. `compareValues` itself places absent values before every present value. Present values of the same type compare as follows: numbers numerically, with `-0` equal to `0`; strings by Unicode code point, so a code point above the basic plane sorts after `U+FFFD` and never by UTF-16 code unit, and never with `localeCompare`; booleans with `false` before `true`. When one key holds several types, order by type: numbers, then strings, then booleans. Any other type of value — an object, an array, a function, a bigint, a symbol — raises `TypeError` with message `unsupported value type: object`, naming the offending `typeof`.

Validation happens before any comparison. Rows that are not an array raise `TypeError` with message `rows must be an array`. A spec list that is not a non-empty array raises `TypeError` with message `at least one key spec is required`. A spec that is not an object raises `TypeError` with message `key spec must be an object`, and one whose key is neither a string nor a function raises `TypeError` with message `key must be a string path or a function`. An unknown direction raises `RangeError` with message `unknown direction: "up"` and an unknown null placement raises `RangeError` with message `unknown null placement: "middle"`, each quoting the offending value as JSON. Do not add dependencies; `test/` and `package.json` are fixed and the suite must pass with `node --test test/*.test.js`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

Implement `src/index.js` so it exports `TableError`, `stringWidth`, `wrapCell`, `padCell` and `formatTable`. `TableError` extends `Error`, sets `name` to `'TableError'`, carries a `code` string, and is constructed as `(code, message)`. Everything below measures text in terminal columns, never in code units, so iterate by code point.

`stringWidth(text)` returns the column count of a string, throwing `'BAD_CELL'` with message `cell must be a string` for a non-string. A code point below U+0020, U+007F, any of U+200B, U+200C, U+200D and U+FEFF, or anything in U+0300 to U+036F counts as 0 columns. A code point in any of these inclusive ranges counts as 2 columns: U+1100-U+115F, U+2E80-U+303E, U+3041-U+33FF, U+3400-U+4DBF, U+4E00-U+9FFF, U+A000-U+A4CF, U+AC00-U+D7A3, U+F900-U+FAFF, U+FE10-U+FE19, U+FE30-U+FE6F, U+FF00-U+FF60, U+FFE0-U+FFE6, U+1F300-U+1F64F, U+1F900-U+1F9FF, U+20000-U+2FFFD and U+30000-U+3FFFD. Everything else counts as 1.

`wrapCell(text, width)` returns the lines a cell occupies in a column of `width` columns, always at least one line, and never a line wider than `width`. `width` must be an integer of at least 1 (`'BAD_WIDTH'`, `width must be a positive integer`) and `text` must be a string (`'BAD_CELL'`, `cell must be a string`). The text is first split on newlines and each piece wrapped on its own, so an empty piece contributes one empty line. Within a piece, runs of one or more spaces separate words and collapse to a single space; leading and trailing spaces disappear, and a piece with no words yields one empty line. A word wider than the column is broken greedily into chunks of at most `width` columns, so a 2-column character that would straddle the edge starts the next chunk and leaves the previous one a column short; a single character wider than the whole column throws `'UNWRAPPABLE'` with message `character is wider than the column`. Words and chunks are then packed greedily, one space between neighbours on the same line, starting a new line whenever the next word would push the line past `width`.

`padCell(text, width, align)` pads one already-fitting line to exactly `width` columns, with `align` defaulting to `'left'` and also accepting `'right'` and `'center'`; centring puts the smaller half of the padding on the left. It throws `'BAD_CELL'` for a non-string, `'BAD_WIDTH'` with message `width must be a positive integer` for a bad width, `'BAD_ALIGN'` with message `unknown alignment: <align>` for anything else, and `'CELL_TOO_WIDE'` with message `content is wider than the column` when the text does not fit. `formatTable(rows, options)` renders `rows`, an array of arrays of strings, using `options.widths` (an array of positive integers, one per column), the optional `options.align` (one alignment per column, all `'left'` by default) and the optional boolean `options.header`. Validation runs in this order, each failure throwing immediately: `options` must be a non-null object (`'BAD_OPTIONS'`, `options must be an object`); `widths` must be a non-empty array of positive integers (`'BAD_WIDTH'`, `widths must be a non-empty array of positive integers`); `align`, when given, must be an array of the same length (`'BAD_ALIGN'`, `align must have <n> entries`) holding known alignments (`'BAD_ALIGN'`, `unknown alignment: <value>`); `rows` must be an array (`'BAD_ROWS'`, `rows must be an array`); and each row, in order, must have one cell per column (`'BAD_ROW_LENGTH'`, `row <i> has <n> cells, expected <m>`, counting a non-array row as 0 cells) with every cell a string (`'BAD_CELL'`, `cell at row <i>, column <j> is not a string`). No rows renders the empty string. Otherwise every cell is wrapped to its column, a row occupies as many lines as its tallest cell with the shorter cells padded out with blanks, and the cells of one line are padded and joined with ` | `. When `header` is true a rule of hyphens per column joined with `-+-` follows the first row. Lines are joined with newlines, with no trailing newline, and every line of the result has the same display width. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

goal.objective:
Implement `src/index.js` so it exports `TableError`, `stringWidth`, `wrapCell`, `padCell` and `formatTable`. `TableError` extends `Error`, sets `name` to `'TableError'`, carries a `code` string, and is constructed as `(code, message)`. Everything below measures text in terminal columns, never in code units, so iterate by code point.

`stringWidth(text)` returns the column count of a string, throwing `'BAD_CELL'` with message `cell must be a string` for a non-string. A code point below U+0020, U+007F, any of U+200B, U+200C, U+200D and U+FEFF, or anything in U+0300 to U+036F counts as 0 columns. A code point in any of these inclusive ranges counts as 2 columns: U+1100-U+115F, U+2E80-U+303E, U+3041-U+33FF, U+3400-U+4DBF, U+4E00-U+9FFF, U+A000-U+A4CF, U+AC00-U+D7A3, U+F900-U+FAFF, U+FE10-U+FE19, U+FE30-U+FE6F, U+FF00-U+FF60, U+FFE0-U+FFE6, U+1F300-U+1F64F, U+1F900-U+1F9FF, U+20000-U+2FFFD and U+30000-U+3FFFD. Everything else counts as 1.

`wrapCell(text, width)` returns the lines a cell occupies in a column of `width` columns, always at least one line, and never a line wider than `width`. `width` must be an integer of at least 1 (`'BAD_WIDTH'`, `width must be a positive integer`) and `text` must be a string (`'BAD_CELL'`, `cell must be a string`). The text is first split on newlines and each piece wrapped on its own, so an empty piece contributes one empty line. Within a piece, runs of one or more spaces separate words and collapse to a single space; leading and trailing spaces disappear, and a piece with no words yields one empty line. A word wider than the column is broken greedily into chunks of at most `width` columns, so a 2-column character that would straddle the edge starts the next chunk and leaves the previous one a column short; a single character wider than the whole column throws `'UNWRAPPABLE'` with message `character is wider than the column`. Words and chunks are then packed greedily, one space between neighbours on the same line, starting a new line whenever the next word would push the line past `width`.

`padCell(text, width, align)` pads one already-fitting line to exactly `width` columns, with `align` defaulting to `'left'` and also accepting `'right'` and `'center'`; centring puts the smaller half of the padding on the left. It throws `'BAD_CELL'` for a non-string, `'BAD_WIDTH'` with message `width must be a positive integer` for a bad width, `'BAD_ALIGN'` with message `unknown alignment: <align>` for anything else, and `'CELL_TOO_WIDE'` with message `content is wider than the column` when the text does not fit. `formatTable(rows, options)` renders `rows`, an array of arrays of strings, using `options.widths` (an array of positive integers, one per column), the optional `options.align` (one alignment per column, all `'left'` by default) and the optional boolean `options.header`. Validation runs in this order, each failure throwing immediately: `options` must be a non-null object (`'BAD_OPTIONS'`, `options must be an object`); `widths` must be a non-empty array of positive integers (`'BAD_WIDTH'`, `widths must be a non-empty array of positive integers`); `align`, when given, must be an array of the same length (`'BAD_ALIGN'`, `align must have <n> entries`) holding known alignments (`'BAD_ALIGN'`, `unknown alignment: <value>`); `rows` must be an array (`'BAD_ROWS'`, `rows must be an array`); and each row, in order, must have one cell per column (`'BAD_ROW_LENGTH'`, `row <i> has <n> cells, expected <m>`, counting a non-array row as 0 cells) with every cell a string (`'BAD_CELL'`, `cell at row <i>, column <j> is not a string`). No rows renders the empty string. Otherwise every cell is wrapped to its column, a row occupies as many lines as its tallest cell with the shorter cells padded out with blanks, and the cells of one line are padded and joined with ` | `. When `header` is true a rule of hyphens per column joined with `-+-` follows the first row. Lines are joined with newlines, with no trailing newline, and every line of the result has the same display width. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.
